title: Annotate each sentence before choosing its picture
when: Turning a narrated script into shots.
summary: Before choosing pictures, read each sentence for what kind of beat it is (a claim, a number, a quote, a turn, a story moment, an instruction), how much weight it carries, which named things it mentions, and what the viewer needs to see to follow it. The picture is chosen from that reading, not from the first noun.
steps: Label the beat type of each sentence.
Mark its weight: a key beat, a supporting beat or a connective.
List the named things and the one thing the viewer needs to see.
Give key beats the strongest visuals and let connective sentences stay simple.
source: video-talkcraft (Vincentwei1021, PolyForm Noncommercial; ideas only, no code or text reused): semantic annotation step; restated.

title: Know the explainer shot types and what each needs
when: Choosing the kind of shot for a beat in a narrated explainer.
summary: Narrated explainers use a small set of shot types, each with its own job: the hook shot (the strongest picture, first 5-8 seconds); the argument or story shot (most of the video); the data shot (a number or chart built on its word); the evidence shot (a document, quote or source shown and pointed at); the multi-evidence shot (two or more sources compared); the punchline or turn shot (one strong statement, big and quiet around it); and the closing shot (the payoff and the rhyme with the opening).
do: Name each shot's type in its notes.
Give data, evidence and turn shots their own composition rather than the story layout.
source: video-talkcraft (PolyForm Noncommercial; ideas only): shot presets; restated.

title: Design every shot in three layers: place, subject, words
summary: A shot has a background layer (the place and one slow camera phrase), a subject layer (one lead per beat, handed on to the next), and a words layer (key words outside the captions, not moved by the camera). Deciding each layer separately keeps shots readable and alive.
do: Give the background one slow camera curve per scene.
Give each beat one lead subject.
Keep the words layer out of the camera's move.
source: video-talkcraft (PolyForm Noncommercial; ideas only): background, subject, text layers; restated.

title: A budget of elements per screen and a whitespace anchor
when: Adding props, words and graphics to a shot.
summary: Screens fill up a little at a time until nothing reads. Give each shot a budget (for example one lead subject, two supporting things and one word element), keep one area of calm space as an anchor for the eye, and keep faces and key subjects out of the caption band.
do: Count the elements of a shot against its budget.
Keep one calm area free.
Keep subjects out of the bottom caption band.
avoid: Adding an element without removing one when the shot is full.
source: video-talkcraft (PolyForm Noncommercial; ideas only): layout discipline; restated.

title: Cut on the sentence that turns the argument
summary: Scene changes land where the argument turns: on 'but', 'so', 'the real reason', a new step or a new place. Cutting in the middle of a thought breaks it; holding through a turn hides it.
do: Change scene on pivot sentences.
Keep one thought inside one scene.
source: video-talkcraft (PolyForm Noncommercial; ideas only): pivot-sentence cut rule; restated.

title: Check three frames around every state change
when: Reviewing a render for glitches a single frame cannot show.
summary: Some defects only exist in time: a one-frame pop, a flash of the wrong state, a word flickering. Look at a burst of three frames just before, at and just after every state change (a cut, an element arriving, a number changing).
steps: Find the state changes from the edit's timeline.
Flag pops, flashes and flickers with their time.
source: video-talkcraft (PolyForm Noncommercial; ideas only): triple-gate review; restated.

title: Rate a moment four ways before turning it into a clip
when: Choosing which moments of a long video become Shorts or highlights.
summary: A good clip scores on four things: information value (a real insight, dense), emotional pull (surprise, anger, curiosity, recognition), spread potential (a line people repeat or argue about) and completeness (it starts and ends on its own).
do: Score candidate moments on the four together.
Prefer moments that start and end at natural pauses.
avoid: A clip that needs the rest of the video to make sense.
source: autoclip_mvp (zhouxiaoka, MIT), pinned ec75aa7: recommendation prompt; restated.

title: Outline a transcript with full coverage, start and end included
when: Reading a long transcript (a reference video or the program's own narration) to find its topics.
summary: When outlining a transcript, cover at least 95% of what matters, including the opening minutes and the ending, which often hold the key claims. Each topic has its points and its start and end time at natural boundaries.
steps: Split the transcript into topics in order.
Place each topic's start and end on pauses or turns.
Put anything left into an 'other points' topic rather than dropping it.
source: autoclip_mvp (MIT), pinned ec75aa7: outline and time-point prompts; restated.

title: Probe first, plan from real numbers, check after, look at the frames
when: Any change to video or audio files.
summary: Plan from measured facts (duration, frame rate, size, loudness), never assumptions. Prefer the lossless path when a cut or remux is enough. Chain steps in a fixed order: colour, cut, join, silence, fit, captions and overlays, sync, audio, loudness, export. Then verify the numbers and look at a contact sheet of the result.
steps: Keep the order colour, cut, join, silence, fit, overlays, sync, audio, loudness, export.
avoid: Re-encoding when a lossless cut does the job.
Rewriting caption words to make them fit.
source: ffmpeg-skill (kajisho5, MIT), pinned 6e42a79: workflow and what the tool does not decide; restated.

title: Drive motion from the frame number, eased and clamped
summary: Every value comes from the current frame: map a frame range to a value range, clamp at both ends so nothing overshoots by accident, and shape it with an easing (a spring without bounce for pushes, a soft bezier for slides). Nothing depends on the wall clock, so any frame renders the same at any time.
do: Compute values from the frame, never from a timer.
Clamp ranges unless an overshoot is intended.
Use a spring without bounce for pushes and reveals.
avoid: Values that keep growing past their range.
source: Remotion agent skills (ideas only; Remotion needs a company licence above three people): timing and interpolation; restated.

title: Measure words before placing them
when: Placing titles, labels and big words.
summary: Text that is fitted by guesswork gets cut off or overflows on long words. Measure the rendered width of the words in their font, fit the size to the space, and leave margins.
do: Fit text size to the measured width.
Leave a margin inside the frame and around neighbours.
source: Remotion agent skills (ideas only): measuring text; restated.

title: 3D scenes that are deterministic and seekable
when: A designed shot uses perspective or 3D-like depth.
summary: Depth scenes for video must give the same picture for the same frame whatever order frames are rendered in: time comes from the frame, never from a clock; camera pitch stays between about 35 and 55 degrees so things never flatten into slabs; layers can separate and recombine with labels pinned to what they name.
do: Derive every position from the frame.
Keep camera pitch moderate and distance safe.
Pin labels to the part they name.
avoid: Repeating textures visible on large surfaces.
source: threejs-skills (CloudAI-X, MIT), pinned 0e18186, and motion-video-kit (MIT) three.js patterns; restated (the program's designed shots stay 2D CSS, GSAP and SVG).
